content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem and sorting out the key facts: memory is climbing and latency is up, but the error rate hasn't moved. The records show no deploys or flag changes beforehand, and a restart is confirmed. My current suspicion is the unbounded _LAST_SEEN dict, and I'm checking whether the U rows showing record_visit on both failure and success paths belong with the others.

I'm treating the U rows as support for part of the hypothesis, since they show record_visit being called on every render, but the unbounded _LAST_SEEN claim still depends on an unverified reading, so the cause rests on something not yet run. There was no change that set it off. For the timeline, I'm starting with what users saw: shop pages grew slow to load, and I'm keeping the first step to the request latency from the metrics read.

Next I'm tracing the memory growth: resident memory climbed steadily toward the container limit while traffic stayed flat, and it dropped back when the process restarted, so I'm pinning the slowdown to the running process rather than to load. I'm also checking that no deploy or flag change lines up with the onset, since the record shows none in the window.

I'm weighing whether any deploy or flag change could explain it, and the records show none in the day before the onset and none in the hour before. I'm also going through the account page render path, where record_visit runs on every render, success or failure, which points toward the growing _LAST_SEEN dict as the likely source.

I'm settling on the root cause: the account page handler calls record_visit on every render, success or failure, and that stores each shopper in a module-level dict that only a restart clears. The part resting on the unverified reading is still the weaker link, so I'll flag it as likely.

I'm weighing a safeguard gap now: the per-shopper store has no size limit or eviction, and no review or test check caught an unbounded process-level store before it shipped.

I'm now weighing the detection gap: the alert that fired was on memory against the limit, and it only triggers after a sustained period, while no alert on request latency was seen. I'm also looking at how the page was routed, since nobody was paged, and noting that Argus caught it within minutes.

I'm working out the contributing factors now, and I'm skipping the candidate rule-outs that the record doesn't actually settle. The latency rise went unflagged by any alert, so I'll note that as a detection gap, and the alert that did fire came too late to be the first signal. Separately, the alert paged nobody, so I'm putting that under what went wrong in the response rather than as a cause.

Next I'm drafting the action items: a review or static check that flags unbounded module-level caches written from request handlers, and a soak test that renders the account page for many distinct shoppers and fails if memory keeps climbing. I'm also adding a latency alert on the shop's request latency, and linking the memory alert to on-call paging so it doesn't go unseen.

I'm noting that the Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop to clear the condition, and it judged the restart confirmed only after the alert stopped firing. The Investigator placed the onset and read the metrics, changes and logs, while Code-Fix proposed a draft PR. The main gap in the response is that the alert paged nobody.

I'm checking the error rates against the normal baseline, which runs around 1%, and seeing that the account page errors before the onset were ordinary. Nothing was really wrong there. The errors stayed flat, so that part didn't drive the incident, but I'm noting that memory got close to the container limit before the restart, and the alert plus the restart stopped it from getting there.

I'm checking the causal chain's first step, which is that shoppers' requests to io-shop were slower to get answers, the slowest ones most of all, while the failure count stayed where it was before.

Next I'm checking the causal chain's second step: memory in the io-shop process kept climbing toward its container limit, and both that and the slowdown cleared once the process was restarted.

I'm building the causal chain now, step by step: the io-shop process kept holding more memory and climbed steadily toward its container limit. Next I'm pinning the cause to memory held inside the running process itself, with no deploy, release, or flag change in the window to explain it, and I'm working through the account page mechanism behind that.

I'm checking the figures in the write-up, keeping any digits limited to names like the PR link and the p95 label, and dropping the bare numeric wording from the draft.

I'm laying out the contributing factors now: first, nothing in review or tests seemed to check that the per-shopper store on the request path was bounded, so it shipped with no limit. Second, no latency alert was seen, so the slowdown was caught only by the memory rule, which waits for its condition to hold before firing.

Now I'm settling on the wording for the symptom line, dropping the awkward first draft and going with something short that names what went wrong for shoppers.

action_items.item: Add a review or static-analysis check that flags module-level dicts, caches or other stores that request handlers write to without a size limit or eviction.
Add a soak test for io-shop that renders account pages for many distinct shoppers and fails if the process's resident memory keeps rising.
Add an alert on io-shop request latency at p95 and p99 against its usual baseline.
Route the io-shop HighMemoryUsage alert to the on-call rotation so that it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: Requests to io-shop took longer to answer, and the slowest requests slowed the most. No more requests failed than usual.
The io-shop process held more and more memory, climbing steadily toward its container limit.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or flag change on the service in the day before the onset: none was recorded.
A flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before Argus checked, which covers the onset: the flag provider's history showed none.

causal_chain.step: The memory was being held inside the running process itself. Nothing was changed in production: no deploy, release or flag change was recorded, and the growth cleared once the process was fresh.

Every account-page render calls record_visit, on success and on failure. Code-Fix's reading is that record_visit adds the shopper to a module-level dict that only forget_every_visit() empties, so the dict gains an entry for every new shopper and is not emptied until the process restarts.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop's server likely keeps a note of every shopper who opens their account page and never throws any of those notes away, so its memory filled up steadily and the shop got slower.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen, in review or in tests, that a store the request path writes to has a size limit. The per-shopper store reached production with no cap and no eviction.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The unbounded store would have been caught before it went out, so memory would not have grown in production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No alert on request latency was seen. The slowdown was found only by the memory rule, which fires only after its condition has held for {rule_waits}.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on the slower requests could have caught the incident sooner and shortened it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

got_lucky: Memory had not yet reached the container limit when the service was put back. At its worst it stood at {series_at_worst} of the limit.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the onset from the service's metrics.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else, which ruled out a flag flip as the trigger.
The Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop to act on C1.
The Mitigation Agent judged the restart confirmed once the service was no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/435.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert.

input.root_cause: serve_account_page calls record_visit on every account-page render, on success and in its exception handler. Code-Fix's reading is that record_visit adds each shopper to `_LAST_SEEN`, a module-level dict in `src/io_shop/visits.py` that only `forget_every_visit()` empties. That means the dict gains an entry for every new shopper and keeps growing in the running process until the process restarts.
input.still_at_risk: The per-shopper store can keep growing with every new shopper, and memory can climb back toward the container limit and slow requests again.
input.symptom: Shop requests slowed down for shoppers
